```{r}
library(tidyverse)

library(SuperLearner)
library(randomForestSRC)

lapply(list.files(here::here("R"), full.names = T), source)

# Set seed for reproducibility 
seed <- 2026
set.seed(seed)
n <- 1000
R <- 10
```

# Scenario 1: Additive hazards 

## Objectives

This scenario: 

* evaluates the overall performance of the VIM procedure under additive hazards: bias, confidence interval coverage, confidence interval width, rejection probability 
* assesses the robustness of the VIM procedure to nuisance-model choice required for VIM computation: Aalen model (`timereg::aalen`), survival Super Learner  (`survivalSL::survivalSL`), global survival stacking (`survML::stackG`)

## Data generation 

Four binary covariates were generated *independently* with prevalences spanning 
rare to frequent alterations, $X_j \sim Bernoulli(0.4)$. 

Events times were simulated under the following the additive hazards 
model: 

$$\lambda(t|x)=\lambda_0(t)+\alpha_{1}(t)X_{1}+\alpha_{2}(t)X_{2}+\alpha_{3}(t)X_{3}+\alpha_{4}(t)X_{4}+\alpha_{5}(t)X_{5}$$

with $\lambda_0(t)=0.05$ (constant) and $\alpha_j(t)=(0.3, 0.15, 0.05, 0.005, 0)$. 

Independent censoring times were generated as $C \sim Uniform(0, c_{max})$. The
parameter $c_{max}$ was calibrated using a large Monte Carlo sample from the 
data-generating mechanism to achieve an expected censoring proportion of 
approximately 20%, and the calibrated value was then fixed across all 
simulation replicates. 

```{r}
c_max_s1 <- calibration_param$params_1$c_max
data_s1 <- generate_data(n        = n, 
                         scenario = "1",
                         c_max    = c_max_s1)
head(data_s1)

# Check prevalences
round(colMeans(data_s1 %>% dplyr::select(starts_with("X"))), 3)

# Check censoring rate 
mean(1 - data_s1$event)
```

**Kaplan-Meier**

```{r }
list_form <- c("1",paste0("X",1:p))%>%
  purrr::map(~as.formula(paste("Surv(time,event)~", .x)))
plot_surv(formula = list_form, 
          data = data_s1, 
          legend.title = c("", paste0("X",1:p)))
```

**Aalen model**

```{r}
# Fit the model
aalen_fit <- timereg::aalen(Surv(time, event)~X1+X2+X3+X4+X5, data = data_s1)
summary(aalen_fit)
```

***Test for non-significant effects***

The model estimates the cumulative effects

$$
A_j(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\alpha_j(u)du.
$$

The reported *Supremum test* evaluates $H_0: A_j(t)=0$, meaning the covariate has no effect on the hazard over time. 

Interpretation of the results 

* Intercept: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(aalen_fit$pval.testBeq0[1], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ Baseline hazard is clearly non zero
* $X_1$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(aalen_fit$pval.testBeq0[2], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ Strong evidence that $X_1$ affects the hazard 
* $X_2$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(aalen_fit$pval.testBeq0[3], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ Strong evidence that $X_2$ affects the hazard 
* $X_3$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(aalen_fit$pval.testBeq0[4], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ Strong evidence that $X_3$ affects the hazard 
* $X_4$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(aalen_fit$pval.testBeq0[5], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ No evidence that $X_4$ affects the hazard 
* $X_5$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(aalen_fit$pval.testBeq0[6], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ No evidence that $X_5$ affects the hazard 

***Test for time invariant effects***

Interpretation of the results of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test

Small p-values $rigtharrow$ evidence of time-varying effects. 

* Intercept: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(aalen_fit$pval.testBeqC[1], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ Baseline hazard clearly varies over time
* $X_1$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(aalen_fit$pval.testBeqC[2], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ Strong evidence that effect of $X_1$ changes over time
* $X_2$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(aalen_fit$pval.testBeqC[3], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ Strong evidence that effect of $X_2$ changes over time
* $X_3$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(aalen_fit$pval.testBeqC[4], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ No strong evidence against constant effect
* $X_4$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(aalen_fit$pval.testBeqC[5], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ No evidence of time variation
* $X_5$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(aalen_fit$pval.testBeqC[6], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ No evidence of time variation

```{r }
# Plot the non-parametric cumulative regression coefficients with 95% CI
plot(aalen_fit, ylim = c(-0.5,4))
```

---

We simulated $R=100$ datasets. 

```{r}
test_aalen <- replicate(R, {
  # Generate data 
  data <- generate_data(n        = n, 
                        scenario = "1",
                        c_max    = c_max_s1)
  # Estimate prevalences 
  prev <- colMeans(data %>% dplyr::select(starts_with("X")))%>%
    stats::setNames(paste0("prev_", names(.)))
  # Censoring rate 
  cens_rate <- stats::setNames(mean(1 - data$event), "cens_rate")
  # Fit Aalen model
  fit_obj <- timereg::aalen(Surv(time, event)~X1+X2+X3+X4+X5, data)
  # Tests
  pval_supremum <- fit_obj[["pval.testBeq0"]] 
  names(pval_supremum) <- paste0("pval_supremum_", names(pval_supremum)) 
  pval_KS <- fit_obj[["pval.testBeqC"]] 
  names(pval_KS) <- paste0("pval_KS_", names(pval_KS)) 
  pval_CvM <- fit_obj[["pval.testBeqC.is"]] 
  names(pval_CvM) <- paste0("pval_CvM_", names(pval_CvM))

  c(prev, cens_rate, pval_supremum, pval_KS, pval_CvM)
  }, simplify = F)%>%
  bind_rows

data.frame(colMeans(test_aalen))%>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column()%>%
  kable(col.names = c("Name","Value"))

test_aalen %>%
  dplyr::select(starts_with("pval"))%>%
  dplyr::mutate(across(everything(), ~ifelse(.x<0.05, 1, 0)))%>%
  dplyr::summarise_all(mean)%>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything())%>%
  kable(col.names = c("p-value","Rejection probability"))
```

## Variable importance 

We compare the following approaches for estimating the nuisance functions 
required for VIM computation:

* Aalen additive hazards model (`timereg::aalen`)
* Super Learner for survival prediction (`survivalSL::survivalSL`)
* Global survival stacking (`survML::stackG`)

The approximate population-level predictive performance and non-parametric VIM for Scenario 1 are presented in @tbl-true-vim-s1. 

```{r}
#| tbl-id: "tbl-true-vim-s1"
#| label: "tbl-true-vim-s1"
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Approximate population-level predictive performance and non-parametric variable importance values for Scenario 1 (S1) at the evaluation horizon."

true_param <- readRDS(here::here("outputs/results/mc_truth_param.rds"))
true_param_s1 <- true_param %>%
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "1")

full_model_s1 <- true_param_s1 %>%
  distinct(vim, true_V_full) %>%
  transmute(
    model = "Full model",
    vim,
    performance = true_V_full,
    importance = NA_real_,
    model_order = 0L
  )

reduced_models_s1 <- true_param_s1 %>%
  transmute(
    model = paste0(
      "Without $X_{",
      stringr::str_remove(variable, "^X"),
      "}$"
    ),
    vim,
    performance = true_V_reduced,
    importance = true_vim,
    model_order = readr::parse_number(variable)
  )

tab_s1 <- bind_rows(full_model_s1, reduced_models_s1) %>%
  mutate(
    vim = recode(
      vim,
      "BS(t)"  = "BS",
      "AUC(t)" = "AUC"
    )
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(model, model_order),
    names_from = vim,
    values_from = c(performance, importance),
    names_glue = "{.value}_{vim}"
  ) %>%
  # arrange(model_order) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    model,
    performance_BS,
    importance_BS,
    performance_AUC,
    importance_AUC
  )%>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    across(2:5, ~ifelse(!is.na(.x), 
                        format(round(.x, 3), nsmall = 3), 
                        "—"))
  )%>%
  purrr::set_names(nm = c("Model",
                          "$V_0^{\\mathrm{BS}}(\\tau)$",
                          "$\\psi_{0,j}^{\\mathrm{BS}}(\\tau)$",
                          "$V_0^{\\mathrm{AUC}}(\\tau)$",
                          "$\\psi_{0,j}^{\\mathrm{AUC}}(\\tau)$"))

ft_tab_s1 <- flextable::flextable(tab_s1)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(tab_s1))) {
  ft_tab_s1 <- ft_tab_s1 %>%
    flextable::compose(
      i = i,
      j = "Model",
      value = mixed_paragraph(tab_s1$Model[i]),
      part = "body"
    )
}

for (j in 2:ncol(tab_s1)){
  ft_tab_s1 <- ft_tab_s1 %>%
    flextable::compose(
    j = j, 
    value = mixed_paragraph(names(tab_s1)[j]),
    part = "header"
  )
}

notes <- "$V_0^{\\mathrm{BS}}(\\tau)$: denotes the population-level predictive performance at horizon $\\tau$, defined as the negative Brier score; $\\psi_{0,j}^{\\mathrm{BS}}(\\tau)$: denotes the loss in Brier-score-based predictive performance resulting from the exclusion of $X_j$; $V_0^{\\mathrm{AUC}}(\\tau)$: denotes the population-level cumulative/dynamic AUC at horizon $\\tau$; $\\psi_{0,j}^{\\mathrm{AUC}}(\\tau)$: denotes the loss in cumulative/dynamic AUC resulting from the exclusion of $X_j$."

ft_tab_s1 %>%
  flextable::add_footer_lines(notes)%>%
  flextable::compose(
    value = mixed_paragraph(notes),
    part = "footer"
  )%>%
  flextable::width(width = c(2, rep(1.1, 4)))%>%
  flextable::fontsize(size = 10, part = "footer")
```

We define time horizons, maximum follow-up time and times at which to approximate integrals.

```{r}
time <- data_s1$time
event <- data_s1$event
X <- data_s1 %>% dplyr::select(starts_with("X")) 
indxs <- paste0(1:ncol(X))
tau_s1 <- calibration_param$params_1$tau
approx_times <- sort(unique(c(0, time[event == 1], tau_s1)))
approx_times <- approx_times[approx_times <= max(tau_s1)]
length(approx_times)
```

We generated cross-fitting and sample-splitting folds.

```{r}
folds <- survML:::generate_folds(n = n, V = 5, sample_split = TRUE)
cf_folds <- folds$cf_folds
table(cf_folds)
ss_folds <- folds$ss_folds
table(ss_folds)
```

### Aalen model (`timereg::aalen`)

```{r}
vims_aalen_s1 <- compute_vim(
  time = time, 
  event = event, 
  X = X, 
  indxs = indxs, 
  tau = tau_s1, 
  approx_times = approx_times, 
  cf_folds = cf_folds, 
  ss_folds = ss_folds, 
  nuisance = "aalen"
)

tbl_vim(vims_aalen_s1)
unique(vims_aalen_s1$runtime)
```

### Global survival stacking (`survML::stackG`)

```{r}
vims_stackG_s1 <- compute_vim(
  time = time, 
  event = event, 
  X = X, 
  indxs = indxs, 
  tau = tau_s1, 
  approx_times = approx_times, 
  cf_folds = cf_folds, 
  ss_folds = ss_folds, 
  nuisance = "stackG"
)

tbl_vim(vims_stackG_s1)
unique(vims_stackG_s1$runtime)
```

### Survival Super Learner (`survivalSL::survivalSL`)

```{r}
vims_survivalSL_s1 <- compute_vim(
  time = time, 
  event = event, 
  X = X, 
  indxs = indxs, 
  tau = tau_s1, 
  approx_times = approx_times, 
  cf_folds = cf_folds, 
  ss_folds = ss_folds, 
  nuisance = "survivalSL"
)

tbl_vim(vims_survivalSL_s1)
unique(vims_survivalSL_s1$runtime)
```

### Run simulations with 5 replications

```{r}
run_sims_s1 <- sapply(
  seq_len(R),
  function(i) {
    message(sprintf("Scenario 1 - Replication %d", i))

    do_one(
      n         = n,

perf_sims_s1 <- run_sims_s1 %>%
```

# Scenario 2: Mixed additive and multiplicative hazards

## Objectives 

This scenario: 

* evaluates the overall performance of the VIM procedure under mixed additive and multiplicative hazards: bias, confidence interval coverage, confidence interval width, rejection probability 
* assesses the robustness of the VIM procedure to nuisance-model choice required for VIM computation: Cox-Aalen model (`timereg::cox.aalen`), survival Super Learner (`survivalSL::survivalSL`), global survival stacking  (`survML::stackG`)

## Data generation

The covariates are generated *independently* as follows:
  
* $X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3} \sim \mathcal{B}(0.4)$
* $Z_{1}, Z_{2} \sim \mathcal{B}(0.4)$
* $Z_{3} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$

To generate mixed additive and multiplicative effects, event times were 
simulated under a Cox-Aalen model with constant baseline hazard: 
$\lambda_0(t)=0.05$. Additive effects were assigned to $X_1$, $X_2$ and $X_3$ with 
coefficients $\alpha_{1}=0.3$, $alpha_{2}=0.1$ and $\alpha_{3}=0$, respectively. 
Multiplicative (proportional hazards) effects were assigned to 
$Z_1$, $Z_2$ and $Z_3$ with coefficients $\beta_{1}=1$, $beta_{2}=0.5$ and
$\beta_{3}=0$, corresponding to hazard ratios of approximately 2.72, 1.65 and 1. 

Independent censoring times were generated as $C \sim Uniform(0, c_{max})$. The
parameter $c_{max}$ was calibrated using a large Monte Carlo sample from the 
data-generating mechanism to achieve an expected censoring proportion of 
approximately 20%, and the calibrated value was then fixed across all 
simulation replicates. 

```{r}
c_max_s2 <- calibration_param$params_2$c_max
data_s2 <- generate_data(n        = n, 
                         scenario = "2",
                         c_max    = c_max_s2)

head(data_s2)

# Check prevalences
colMeans(data_s2 %>% dplyr::select(X1:X3,Z1:Z2))

# Check mean and sd 
round(mean(data_s2$Z3), 3)
sd(data_s2$Z3)

# Check censoring rate 
mean(1 - data_s2$event)

cox_aalen_fit <- timereg::cox.aalen(
  Surv(time, event)~X1+X2+X3+prop(Z1)+prop(Z2)+prop(Z3), 
  data = data_s2, n.sim = 1000, basesim = 1
)
summary(cox_aalen_fit)
```

**Kaplan-Meier**

```{r }
list_form <- c("1",paste0("X",1:3), paste0("Z",1:2))%>%
  purrr::map(~as.formula(paste("Surv(time,event)~", .x)))
plot_surv(formula = list_form, 
          data = data_s2, 
          legend.title = c("", paste0("X",1:3), paste0("Z",1:2)))
```

**Cox-Aalen model**

```{r}
# Fit Cox-Aalen model 
cox_aalen_fit <- timereg::cox.aalen(
  Surv(time, event)~X1+X2+X3+prop(Z1)+prop(Z2)+prop(Z3), 
  data = data_s2, n.sim = 1000, basesim = 1)
summary(cox_aalen_fit)
```

***Test for non-significant effects***

* Intercept: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(cox_aalen_fit$pval.testBeq0[1], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ Baseline hazard is clearly non zero
* $X_1$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(cox_aalen_fit$pval.testBeq0[2], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ Strong evidence that $X_1$ affects the hazard 
* $X_2$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(cox_aalen_fit$pval.testBeq0[3], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ No evidence that $X_2$ affects the hazard 
* $X_3$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(cox_aalen_fit$pval.testBeq0[4], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ No evidence that $X_3$ affects the hazard 

***Test for time invariant effects***

* Intercept: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(cox_aalen_fit$pval.testBeqC[1], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ Baseline hazard clearly varies over time
* $X_1$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(cox_aalen_fit$pval.testBeqC[2], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ Strong evidence that $X_1$ affects the hazard 
* $X_2$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(cox_aalen_fit$pval.testBeqC[3], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ No evidence of time variation
* $X_3$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(cox_aalen_fit$pval.testBeqC[4], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ No evidence of time variation

***Test of proportionality***

* $Z_1$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(cox_aalen_fit$pval.Prop[1], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ Compatible with a proportional effect
* $Z_2$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(cox_aalen_fit$pval.Prop[2], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ Compatible with a proportional effect
* $Z_3$: `r gtsummary::style_pvalue(cox_aalen_fit$pval.Prop[3], prepend_p = TRUE)` $\rightarrow$ Compatible with a proportional effect

```{r }
# Plot additive Aalen terms
plot(cox_aalen_fit, ylim = c(-0.5,5))

# Plot multiplicative terms 
plot(cox_aalen_fit,  score= TRUE) 
```

---

We simulated $R=100$ datasets. 

```{r}
test_cox_aalen <- replicate(R, {
  # Generate data 
  data <- generate_data(n        = n, 
                        scenario = "2",
                        c_max    = c_max_s2)
  # Estimate prevalences 
  prev <- colMeans(data %>% dplyr::select(X1:X3,Z1:Z2))%>%
    stats::setNames(paste0("prev_", names(.)))
  # Mean and sd Z3
  mean_sd_Z3 <- stats::setNames(c(mean(data$Z3), sd(data$Z3)),
                                c("mean_Z3","sd_Z3"))
  # Censoring rate 
  cens_rate <- stats::setNames(mean(1 - data$event), "cens_rate")
  # Fit Cox-Aalen model
  fit_obj <- timereg::cox.aalen(
    Surv(time, event)~X1+X2+X3+prop(Z1)+prop(Z2)+prop(Z3),
    data = data, n.sim = 1000, basesim = 1
  )
  # Additive terms 
  pval_supremum <- fit_obj[["pval.testBeq0"]] 
  names(pval_supremum) <- paste0("pval_supremum_", names(pval_supremum)) 
  pval_KS <- fit_obj[["pval.testBeqC"]] 
  names(pval_KS) <- paste0("pval_KS_", names(pval_KS)) 
  # pval_CvM <- fit_obj[["pval.testBeqC.is"]] 
  # names(pval_CvM) <- paste0("pval_CvM", names(pval_CvM))
  # Multiplicative terms 
  coef <- coef(fit_obj)[,"Coef."]
  # Test for proportional 
  pval_prop <- stats::setNames(
    fit_obj$pval.Prop, 
    gsub("prop\\(|\\)","", paste0("pval_prop_", names(fit_obj$pval.Prop)))
    )
  
  c(prev, mean_sd_Z3, cens_rate, 
    pval_supremum, pval_KS, #pval_CvM, 
    coef, pval_prop)
  
  }, simplify = F)%>%
  bind_rows()

data.frame(round(colMeans(test_cox_aalen),3))%>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column()%>%
  kable(col.names = c("Name","Value"))

test_cox_aalen %>%
  dplyr::select(starts_with("pval"))%>%
  dplyr::mutate(across(everything(), ~ifelse(.x<0.05, 1, 0)))%>%
  dplyr::summarise_all(mean)%>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything())%>%
  mutate(value = round(value, 3))%>%
  kable(col.names = c("p-value","Rejection probability"))
```

## Variable importance

We compare the following approaches for estimating the nuisance functions 
required for VIM computation:

* Cox-Aalen model (`timereg::cox.aalen`)
* Survival Super Learner (`survivalSL::survivalSL`)
* Global survival stacking (`survML::stackG`)

The approximate population-level predictive performance and non-parametric VIM for Scenario 2 are presented in @tbl-true-vim-s2. 

```{r}
#| tbl-id: "tbl-true-vim-s2"
#| label: "tbl-true-vim-s2"
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Approximate population-level predictive performance and non-parametric variable importance values for Scenario 2 (S2) at the evaluation horizon."

true_param_s2 <- true_param %>%
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "2")

full_model_s2 <- true_param_s2 %>%
  distinct(vim, true_V_full) %>%
  transmute(
    model = "Full model",
    vim,
    performance = true_V_full,
    importance = NA_real_,
    model_order = 0L
  )

reduced_models_s2 <- true_param_s2 %>%
  transmute(
    model = 
      case_when(
        startsWith(variable, "X") ~
          paste0("Without $X_{", stringr::str_remove(variable, "^X"),"}$"),
        startsWith(variable, "Z") ~
          paste0("Without $Z_{", stringr::str_remove(variable, "^Z"),"}$"),
    ),
    vim,
    performance = true_V_reduced,
    importance = true_vim,
    model_order = readr::parse_number(model)
  )

tab_s2 <- bind_rows(full_model_s2, reduced_models_s2) %>%
  mutate(
    vim = recode(
      vim,
      "BS(t)"  = "BS",
      "AUC(t)" = "AUC"
    )
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(model, model_order),
    names_from = vim,
    values_from = c(performance, importance),
    names_glue = "{.value}_{vim}"
  ) %>%
  # arrange(model_order) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    model,
    performance_BS,
    importance_BS,
    performance_AUC,
    importance_AUC
  )%>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    across(2:5, ~ifelse(!is.na(.x), 
                        format(round(.x, 3), nsmall = 3), 
                        "—"))
  )%>%
  purrr::set_names(nm = c("Model",
                          "$V_0^{\\mathrm{BS}}(\\tau)$",
                          "$\\psi_{0,j}^{\\mathrm{BS}}(\\tau)$",
                          "$V_0^{\\mathrm{AUC}}(\\tau)$",
                          "$\\psi_{0,j}^{\\mathrm{AUC}}(\\tau)$"))

ft_tab_s2 <- flextable::flextable(tab_s2)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(tab_s2))) {
  ft_tab_s2 <- ft_tab_s2 %>%
    flextable::compose(
      i = i,
      j = "Model",
      value = mixed_paragraph(tab_s2$Model[i]),
      part = "body"
    )
}

for (j in 2:ncol(tab_s2)){
  ft_tab_s2 <- ft_tab_s2 %>%
    flextable::compose(
    j = j, 
    value = mixed_paragraph(names(tab_s2)[j]),
    part = "header"
  )
}

notes <- "$V_0^{\\mathrm{BS}}(\\tau)$: denotes the population-level predictive performance at horizon $\\tau$, defined as the negative Brier score; $\\psi_{0,j}^{\\mathrm{BS}}(\\tau)$: denotes the loss in Brier-score-based predictive performance resulting from the exclusion of $X_j$; $V_0^{\\mathrm{AUC}}(\\tau)$: denotes the population-level cumulative/dynamic AUC at horizon $\\tau$; $\\psi_{0,j}^{\\mathrm{AUC}}(\\tau)$: denotes the loss in cumulative/dynamic AUC resulting from the exclusion of $X_j$."

ft_tab_s2 %>%
  flextable::add_footer_lines(notes)%>%
  flextable::compose(
    value = mixed_paragraph(notes),
    part = "footer"
  )%>%
  flextable::width(width = c(2, rep(1.1, 4)))%>%
  flextable::fontsize(size = 10, part = "footer")
```

We define time horizons, maximum follow-up time and times at which to approximate integrals.

```{r}
time <- data_s2$time
event <- data_s2$event
X <- data_s2 %>% dplyr::select(starts_with(c("X","Z"))) 
indxs <- paste0(1:ncol(X))
tau_s2 <- calibration_param$params_2$tau
approx_times <- sort(unique(c(0, time[event == 1], tau_s2)))
approx_times <- approx_times[approx_times <= max(tau_s2)]
length(approx_times)
```

We generated cross-fitting and sample-splitting folds.

```{r}
folds <- survML:::generate_folds(n = n, V = 5, sample_split = TRUE)
cf_folds <- folds$cf_folds
table(cf_folds)
ss_folds <- folds$ss_folds
table(ss_folds)
```

```{r}
vims_cox_aalen_s2 <- compute_vim(

  cf_folds = cf_folds, 
  ss_folds = ss_folds, 
  nuisance = "cox.aalen"

tbl_vim(vims_cox_aalen_s2)
```

# Additional numerical experiments

## Sensitivity to low-prevalence covariates

### Objectives

An additional scenario was designed to evaluate the overall performance of the procedure used to estimate intrinsic variable importance measures in the presence of low-prevalence covariates with heterogeneous prognostic effects, ranging from no effect to a strong effect.

More specifically, the objective is to assess whether the VIM approach can:

* detect rare yet highly prognostic alterations,
* discriminate between weak and strong prognostic signals, and
* correctly identify non-informative (null) variables.

### Data generating mechanism

Across all simulations, event times were generated according to a conditional exponential model:

$$
T_i\mid X_i,Z_i\sim\operatorname{Exp}(r_i),
$$

where $r_i$ denotes the event rate conditional on the covariates. Two parameterizations of this rate were considered: a purely additive structure and a mixed Cox–Aalen structure combining additive and multiplicative effects.

The covariates were generated using different combinations of marginal prevalences and effect sizes, as presented in @tbl-sims-prev. These additional experiments therefore allowed us to investigate the sensitivity of the procedure to low covariate prevalence and heterogeneity in the prognostic signal.

```{r}
#| tbl-id: "tbl-sims-prev"
#| label: "tbl-sims-prev"
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Simulation settings assessing sensitivity to low-prevalence covariates."

tab_sims_prev <- data.frame(
  prev = c(
    rep("Very rare", 3),
    rep("Rare", 3)
  ),
  pi_j = c(
    rep("0.01", 3),
    rep("0.10", 3)),
  effect = rep(c("Strong", "Moderate", "Null"), 2),
  alpha = rep(c(0.1, 0.05, 0), 2),
  beta = rep(c(1, 0.5, 0), 2)
)

colnames <- c("Prevalence category",
              "$\\pi_j$",
              "Effect category",
              "$\\alpha$",
              "$\\beta$")

ft_tab_sims_prev <- tab_sims_prev %>%
  flextable::flextable() 

for (j in 1:ncol(tab_sims_prev)){
  ft_tab_sims_prev <- ft_tab_sims_prev %>%
    flextable::compose(
    j = j, 
    value = mixed_paragraph(colnames[j]),
    part = "header"
  )
}

notes <- "$\\pi_j$: marginal prevalence of covariate $j$; $\\alpha$: constant additive effect on the hazard scale; $\\beta$: multiplicative effect on the log-hazard scale. Effect levels were classified as null, intermediate, or strong."

ft_tab_sims_prev %>%
  flextable::add_footer_lines(notes)%>%
  flextable::compose(
    value = mixed_paragraph(notes),
    part = "footer"
  )%>%
  flextable::fontsize(size = 10, part = "footer")%>%
  flextable::width(width = 6.3/5)
```

## Sensitivity to covariate correlations

For each scenario, we also assessed the sensitivity of the estimated nonparametric variable importance measure to correlations among the covariates. Dependence was introduced among selected covariates while preserving their marginal distributions, whether binary or continuous. Two levels of dependence were considered: moderate correlation, set at $\rho=0.6$, and strong correlation, set at $\rho=0.8$. For continuous covariates, these values correspond to Pearson correlation coefficients. For binary covariates, they correspond to the latent correlations of the Gaussian copula used to generate them.

This analysis allowed us to assess the ability of the estimates to recover the population-level reference values when prognostic information is partially shared among several covariates.
